@setup subject=Physics grade=12 topic="RLC circuits"

Good morning everyone. Today we will study circuits with resistors, inductors and capacitors.
[pause 1]
An inductor opposes a change in current, and a capacitor stores charge on its plates.
This idea resonates with what we saw last week about energy storage.
[pause 1.5]
Consider a series RLC circuit switched on to a 10 volt battery.
R is 10 ohms, L is 10 millihenry and C is 100 microfarads.
[pause 1]
When the switch is closed the current rises, the capacitor charges and the voltage overshoots.
Because the damping is small the circuit is underdamped, so the capacitor voltage oscillates before it settles.
In a parallel RLC circuit the behaviour is different, but we will not do that today.
[pause 1]
Let's look at the graph of the capacitor voltage.
[pause 1.5]
Okay, let's get back to the slides.
[pause 1]
The damping ratio depends on R, L and C, and a larger resistance means more damping.
[pause 1.5]
Now consider an LCR circuit connected to a 10 volt, 50 hertz AC supply.
The resistance is 10 ohms, the inductance is 0.1 henry and the capacitance is 100 microfarads.
[pause 1]
The inductive and capacitive reactances nearly cancel, so the current is close to its largest value.
At the resonant frequency the impedance equals the resistance.
[pause 1.5]
Okay, let's get back to the slides.
[pause 1]
Resonance is used in radio tuning circuits to pick one station.
